title: India Demands Global Scrutiny of Pakistan's Crackdown in PoK as Death Toll Mounts
excerpt: More than 32 people killed in clashes as Islamabad bans protest coalition under anti-terror laws, with India and rights groups calling for a UN investigation.
body:
• India has called on the international community to hold Pakistan accountable for alleged human rights abuses in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, where more than 32 people have been killed in clashes.
  • The Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a coalition demanding political reforms, has been banned by Pakistani authorities under anti-terrorism legislation.
  • International human rights organizations have called for a UN-led fact-finding mission into the crackdown, citing documented civilian deaths, arbitrary arrests, and communications blackouts.
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs accused Pakistan of running a fake news campaign to divert attention from its brutality against PoK protesters.

India's Sharpest Rebuke

India has sharply criticized Pakistan over reports of deadly violence in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, accusing Islamabad of concealing its failures through a campaign of misinformation and calling on the international community to hold the country accountable.

Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said there was a pattern of fake news and videos emanating from Pakistan, describing it as a desperate attempt to cover up human rights abuses. The comments came as clashes between protesters and security forces across PoK left more than 32 people dead and over 200 injured.

"There are reports of severe police brutality in Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir in which several protesters have been killed and many injured. We hope the international community will hold Pakistan accountable for its misdeeds and abuses."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

The JAAC Movement

The violence was triggered after Pakistan's regional administration banned the Joint Awami Action Committee under anti-terrorism laws. The JAAC, a coalition of traders, transporters, lawyers, and student groups, had been organizing demonstrations across PoK around a 38-point charter of demands.

The demands include subsidized essential goods, electoral reforms, and the abolition of 12 reserved assembly seats for Kashmiri refugees who settled in Pakistan after 1947. The JAAC alleges these seats have been exploited by mainstream Pakistani political parties to manipulate government formation in Muzaffarabad.

The unrest began in 2023 over high electricity tariffs and flour shortages but has since expanded into a broader movement challenging Pakistan's control over the region. The International Human Rights Foundation documented a recurring pattern of deadly crackdowns, including violence in May 2024 and October 2025.

Calls for UN Investigation

At the 62nd Session of the UN Human Rights Council, India exercised its right of reply to reject Pakistan's allegations about Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the territory was, is, and will always remain an integral part of India.

Meanwhile, international rights organizations have intensified calls for an independent UN-led fact-finding mission. The documented civilian deaths, arbitrary arrests of more than 100 activists, detention of journalists, and communications blackouts across the region constitute a compelling case for international scrutiny, according to reports from the International Human Rights Foundation and other monitoring groups.

Pakistan's own Human Rights Commission expressed alarm at the ongoing violence, voicing serious concerns about the regional government's decision to proscribe the JAAC under anti-terrorism legislation.

A Pattern of Escalation

The PoK crisis highlights long-standing tensions in a region that has remained disputed since the 1947 partition. For India, the crackdown validates its narrative that Pakistan is unable to govern the territory it controls. For Islamabad, the protests represent an internal security challenge compounded by economic pressures.

Internet and mobile networks were suspended across PoK during the unrest, and federal paramilitary troops were deployed alongside local security forces. Journalist Sohrab Barkat was detained under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act.
nri_angle: Kashmiri diaspora communities in the US and UK closely monitor the PoK crisis, with the escalating violence fueling both diplomatic engagement and community activism abroad.
